label: lem:integral_is_antiderivative
title: The integral function is an antiderivative
statement: Let $f : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous on $[\min(a,b), \max(a,b)]$. Then the function $G(u) = \int_a^u f(t)\,dt$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on $(\min(a,b), \max(a,b))$, i.e., $\texttt{IsAntiderivativeOn}\; G\; f\; (\min(a,b))\; (\max(a,b))$.
proof: By the First FTC (Theorem~\ref{thm:ftc1}), for every $x \in (\min(a,b), \max(a,b))$, the function $G(u) = \int_a^u f(t)\,dt$ has derivative $f(x)$ at $x$. By Definition~\ref{def:antiderivative}, this means $G$ is an antiderivative of $f$ on $(\min(a,b), \max(a,b))$.
